content:
My first loaf was dense enough to serve as a doorstop, but its crust smelled wonderful and convinced me to keep trying. Over the next month I changed only one variable at a time, recording water temperature, room temperature, folding intervals, and the appearance of the starter.

The useful breakthrough was not a special flour or an expensive oven. It was learning to watch the dough rather than the clock. On cold mornings fermentation took hours longer, while a warm afternoon could make the same dough move surprisingly quickly.

A recipe is a map, but the dough still tells you where you are.

Thirty loaves later, I still make uneven bread, yet every loaf now has an open crumb and a crisp crust. The notes matter because they turn each mistake into information for the next attempt, instead of a reason to begin again from memory.
